sentences.text: The species name turdirostris was chosen because the bird had a beak shape similar to that of a thrush, featuring a long, slender beak and body proportions akin to the modern varied thrush.

Unlike modern thrushes, Palaeoscinis had relatively short legs that were shorter than its wing bones, while the claw on the reversed first toe was long, measuring approximately 70% of the length of the preceding toe bone.

The extinct songbird genus Palaeoscinis was described in 1957 from fossils found in the middle Miocene Monterey Formation of Santa Barbara, California, discovered in 1955 on limestone slabs originally intended to be used as flagstones.
Its short legs relative to its wings suggest it may have been less adapted for ground running than for perching or climbing.

Palaeoscinis was placed in its own family due to unique skeletal characteristics of the sternum, shoulder, and humerus, as well as proportions unlike any known songbird family, though Wetmore (1960) provisionally allocated it as closest to the Pycnonotidae based on proportions, although this relationship remains uncertain.
Palaeoscinis lived during the Langhian to Serravallian stages, from 15.98 to 11.63 million years ago.

Howard (1957) suggested Palaeoscinis might be related to bulbuls, waxwings, corvids, or dippers, though this relationship is not certain, while Wetmore (1960) provisionally allocated Palaeoscinis as closest to the Pycnonotidae based on proportions, although this relationship remains uncertain.
